what: PORT-7's question (N6, the incremental engine): what a native incremental planner would save. Per scale of the planner audit fixture (bcir.tests.planner_fixtures.audit_fixture), seven one-claim deltas (bcir.tests.delta_fixtures.audit_delta, the delta-ratio row's own); the oracle's optimize from scratch, the oracle's IncrementalPlan.apply, and the C planner's whole plan (bcir_kp_plan, test_kplan --bench, the native planner row's harness) of the final module
host: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.10GHz, 4 vCPU, a virtual machine; Linux 6.18; Python 3.11.15; test_kplan built by tools/c/check_runtime.sh (clang 18.1.3, -O2)
method: medians: time.perf_counter around one call, gc collected before each, seven deltas a scale; the C plan the median of nine rounds of repeated calls (test_kplan --bench). Wall class on a shared virtual machine: INDICATIVE only, never a gate
reading: The C planner plans from scratch at about 0.32 microseconds a claim (10.5 ms at 32,768 claims); the oracle's incremental planner applies a one-claim delta in 0.18 to 2.1 ms, below the C planner's whole plan from 4,096 claims on. A native incremental planner would save at most the C whole plan per delta (10.5 ms at 32,768 claims) to a consumer that re-plans natively from declared deltas.

records.measure.py: the script that produced the rows: python3 measure.py <test_kplan>
